# Unmarked Exits

There is a last time for everything, and almost none of them are announced.

Somewhere in your past is the final afternoon your mother picked you up and carried you on her hip. It didn't feel final. Her arms didn't know. The day simply arrived when you were too heavy, or too proud, or already walking everywhere on your own, and the carrying stopped forever. No one said, *this is the last time.* The last time you were carried is among the more significant days of your life, and it left no trace in your memory.

This is the ordinary shape of endings. They don't knock. They don't leave a note. They happen on a Tuesday, in the middle of a sentence, while you're thinking about something else.

The last time you jumped off the low dive at the town pool. The last time all four of your grandparents were alive in the world — you were probably complaining about dinner. The last time you played with a friend whose name you now have to pause to retrieve. The last time you walked through a particular door — a store, a school, a kitchen — believing you would walk through it again. Then the store closed, or the friend moved away, or you grew up and out, and the door became an image, then a story, then barely a story.

We're good at marking the endings we can see coming. Graduations. Farewell parties. The last day at a job, the night before a friend moves overseas. We buy cakes. We give speeches. We take a picture of everyone waving. These endings are almost easy, because they let us rehearse.

The ones that matter more are the ones that were already over before we noticed. The last time the whole family was in one house at once. The last time you were bored in the specific way only a summer afternoon as a child can make you bored — that endless, golden boredom that will never visit you again in the same form. You were there for it. You just didn't know it was a departure.

Photographs understand this before we do. Nobody treasures the posed birthday pictures quite the way they treasure the accidental ones — the blurry shot of a kitchen on a morning when nothing was happening, someone laughing at something off-frame, a now-gone dog asleep in a patch of light. The photo that seemed like nothing at the time becomes the one that stops your heart later, because it happens to be the last photograph of a version of the world that ended without filing a change-of-address form.

The same silence attends the larger exits.

When Boa Sr died in 2010, a language died with her. She was the last fluent speaker of Aka-Bo, one of the Great Andamanese languages of the Bay of Bengal — a language spoken for thousands of years, with names for things no other language will ever again have names for. Toward the end she sang, and the recordings remain. A whole way of being human, compressed into one elderly woman's voice, and then not even that.

In 1987, on the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi, the last ʻōʻō sang into a microphone. These birds sang duets. The male calls, the female answers, the two voices braided together in the forest. This last one was a male, and he sang both parts, because that is how the duet goes. There was no one left to answer. If you listen to the recording, you can hear him offer the female's line into the empty air, wait, and try again. He may have been the only creature on Earth who still remembered the whole song.

Even the sky keeps quiet exits. The moon is drifting away from us at about four centimeters a year — the slow leak of the tides. In roughly six hundred million years, the moon will be too far away to cover the sun completely, and there will be a last total solar eclipse. No one will bake a cake. No one will warn the Earth. The shadow will simply cross for the final time, and after that, for as long as the planet lasts, a ring of fire where a miracle used to be.

I don't say any of this to be morbid. Or rather, I do, but melancholy and attention are close cousins, and the second is more useful. You cannot mark the unmarked exits in advance; that's what makes them what they are. What you can do is walk into the rooms you're still in more fully. The ordinary Tuesday you're sitting in right now — the specific light, the specific annoyances, whoever is still alive and reachable on your phone — is already, in ways you cannot know, becoming a time you will miss. Most of what you will ever lose is things you aren't even sure you'd notice losing.

So this is not an elegy. It's a reminder to look up. The last times are happening all around us, quietly, all the time, and the only available response is a kind of fierce attention to the present tense — not because it is permanent, but because it isn't. The carrying, the low dive, the door, the duet, the shadow of the moon: all of it was ordinary until it was over, and then it was the whole world.

Pay attention on the Tuesdays. That's where everything ends, and where almost everything happens.

**Unmarked Exits**

There is a last time for everything, and almost none of them are announced.

Somewhere in your past is the final afternoon your mother picked you up and carried you on her hip. It didn't feel final. Her arms didn't know. The day simply arrived when you were too heavy, or too proud, or already walking everywhere on your own, and the carrying stopped forever. No one said, this is the last time. The last time you were carried is among the more significant days of your life, and it left no trace in your memory.

This is the ordinary shape of endings. They don't knock. They don't leave a note. They happen on a Tuesday, in the middle of a sentence, while you're thinking about something else.

The last time you jumped off the low dive at the town pool. The last time all four of your grandparents were alive in the world — you were probably complaining about dinner. The last time you played with a friend whose name you now have to pause to retrieve. The last time you walked through a particular door — a store, a school, a kitchen — believing you would walk through it again. Then the store closed, or the friend moved away, or you grew up and out, and the door became an image, then a story, then barely a story.

We're good at marking the endings we can see coming. Graduations. Farewell parties. The last chemo session, the last day at a job, the night before a friend moves overseas. We buy cakes. We give speeches. We take a picture of everyone waving. These endings are almost easy, because they let us rehearse.

The ones that matter more are the ones that were already over before we noticed. The last time the whole family was in one house at once. The last time you were bored in the specific way only a summer afternoon as a child can make you bored — that endless, golden boredom that will never visit you again in the same form. You were there for it. You just didn't know it was a departure.

Photographs understand this before we do. Nobody treasures the posed birthday pictures quite the way they treasure the accidental ones — the blurry shot of a kitchen on a morning when nothing was happening, someone laughing at something off-frame, a now-gone dog asleep in a patch of light. The photo that seemed like nothing at the time becomes the one that stops your heart later, because it happens to be the last photograph of a version of the world that ended without filing a change-of-address form.

The same silence attends the larger exits.

When Boa Sr died in 2010, a language died with her. She was the last fluent speaker of Aka-Bo, one of the Great Andamanese languages of the Bay of Bengal — a language that had been spoken for thousands of years, that had names for things no other language would ever again have names for. Toward the end she sang, and the recordings remain. A whole way of being human compressed into one elderly woman's voice, and then not even that.

In 1987, on the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi, the last ʻōʻō sang into a microphone. The Kauaʻi ʻōʻō sang duets. The male calls, the female answers, the two voices braided together in the forest. This last one was a male, and he sang both parts, because that is how the duet goes. There was no one left to answer. If you listen to the recording you can hear him offer the female's line into the empty air, wait, and try again. He may have been the only creature on Earth who still remembered the whole song.

Even the sky keeps quiet exits. The moon is drifting away from us at about four centimeters a year — the slow leak of the tides. In roughly six hundred million years, the moon will be too far away to cover the sun completely, and there will be a last total solar eclipse. No one will make a cake. No one will warn the Earth. The shadow will simply cross for the final time, and after that, for as long as the planet lasts, a ring of fire where a miracle used to be.

I don't say any of this to be morbid. Or rather, I do, but melancholy and attention are close cousins, and the second is more useful. You cannot mark the unmarked exits in advance; that's what makes them what they are. What you can do is walk into the rooms you're still in more fully. The ordinary Tuesday you're sitting in right now — the specific light, the specific annoyances, whoever is still alive and reachable on your phone — is already, in ways you cannot know, becoming a time you will miss. Most of what you will ever lose is things you aren't even sure you'd notice losing.

So this is not an elegy. It's a reminder to look up. The last times are happening all around us, quietly, all the time, and the only available response to that fact is a kind of fierce attention to the present tense — not because it is permanent, but because it isn't. The carrying, the low dive, the door, the duet, the shadow of the moon: all of it was ordinary until it was over, and then it was the whole world.

Pay attention on the Tuesdays. That's where everything ends, and where almost everything happens.
